newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: INTERVIEW - S.Lanka Telecom upbeat on NTT tie-up.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - S.Lanka Telecom upbeat on NTT tie-up.

text.p: Sri Lanka Telecom will be able to compete better with its rivals following a strategic partnership with Japan's Nippon Telephone and Telegraphic Corp (NTT), its chairman said on Wednesday.
"We needed this change and we have got it," Hemasiri Fernando told Reuters in an interview.
NTT bought a 35 percent stake and management in Sri Lanka Telecom (SLT) on Tuesday for $225 million, making it the biggest single foreign investment in the Indian Ocean island.
Fernando said SLT, which had a monopoly on telecommunications services in Sri Lanka until very recently, was unable to meet the pent-up demand for phones since it was state-owned.
"We have had the monopoly of telecom in Sri Lanka for decades, but since independence (in 1948) up to now we have only provided 300,000 land-based lines, which is a negligible number," he said.

"We had to always follow government procedures and tender rules and it was not possible to meet up with existing demand," Fernando said, adding that there was a waiting list of 300,000 applicants for telephones in Sri Lanka.

Fernando said other private telecom companies offering mobile and wireless local loop (WLL) telephones in Sri Lanka had distinct advantages over SLT since they received concessions like duty free imports of equipment and income tax rebates.
He said SLT expected to get some of those concessions through NTT, which was now the biggest foreign investor in Sri Lanka.
"If we were a monopoly it would not have bothered us. But the situation is different and to be competitive we need certain facilities," he said.
Fernando said SLT also had a huge workforce of nearly 9,000 people and ran 300 exchanges on the island compared to smaller staff and fewer exchanges run by private phone companies.
"We are facing unfair competition," he said.
Fernando said SLT had seven network expansion projects worth 21 billion rupees ($357 million) in hand. They should be completed in the next two-three years and will double capacity to 600,000 lines.
Few other projects were being implemented with funding from the World Bank and other multilateral agencies, Fernando said.
NTT's arrival should further help the expansion, Fernando said. He did not give details.
Sri Lanka, which allowed mobile phone companies in the country in late 1980s, permitted two WLL operators -- Sweden's Telia AB and Bell Canada -- in 1996 to meet the rising demand.
The two companies are expected to each invest $100 million and provide up to 200,000 lines in total by 2000.
There are 75,000 mobile phones in Sri Lanka.
Fernando said he expected a million telephones in Sri Lanka in 2000, with SLT's share at 75 percent of the market. ($1=58.8 rupees)
